A German noun can have two different sed.why: "Sedge-mark" is a made-up word property (catalogued as has_sedge_mark, fictional, no property tags). It names no real feature of nouns, so a model has no default reading of it as one-valued (as it has for gender) and nothing to contradict.

The past tense of 'sing' is 'sang'..why: True: the standard example of vowel-gradation verbs.

sources.query: past tense of sing is sang

Greek is a Slavic language..why: Deliberately false so the disjunction turns on the inserted property: Greek forms its own Hellenic branch, not Slavic.

notes: RBox expansion paired with grammar-replace-0018 (the revision denies that has_gender is functional on '-ung' nouns). A made-up property, 'has the sedge-mark', is declared not functional and applied to German '-ung' nouns that the revision does not use (Hoffnung, Meinung), with the first mark given in the prompt. The first instance asks whether a second mark is possible (yes, also asked in Chinese and Spanish), the second whether the fact rules one out (no). Near asks the same property of real German gender on '-heit' nouns, which stay one-gendered (yes); far an unrelated symmetric relation. Side facts: the past tense of 'sing', and a false language-family claim.
